title: Vector Stores & Indexes
summary: Once documents are chunked and embedded, you need somewhere to store those vectors and search them fast. A vector store holds each vector with its text and metadata and answers 'give me the top-k most similar to this query'. Comparing the query against every vector (brute force) is exact but slow at scale, so stores use approximate nearest-neighbor indexes like HNSW and IVF to trade a little accuracy for huge speed. You also filter by metadata to scope results. This is the retrieval engine at the heart of RAG.

subtopics.title: A vector store holds vectors, text, and metadata
subtopics.explanation: A vector store is a database specialized for embeddings: each record is a vector plus the original text and its metadata, keyed by a stable id. You 'upsert' chunk records at index time and 'query' with an embedded question at search time. Keeping the vector, text, and metadata together is what lets a single query return rankable, citable, filterable results.
subtopics.example:
store = VectorStore(dim=384)
store.upsert([
    {"id": "doc.md::c0", "vector": embed("refunds take 14 days"),
     "text": "refunds take 14 days", "metadata": {"product": "pro"}},
    {"id": "doc.md::c1", "vector": embed("store opens at 9am"),
     "text": "store opens at 9am", "metadata": {"product": "pro"}},
])
# query time: embed the question, ask for nearest vectors
hits = store.query(embed("how long for a refund"), k=1)

subtopics.title: Brute force vs approximate search
subtopics.explanation: Exact search compares the query to every stored vector and returns the true nearest neighbors, but its cost grows linearly with the corpus, becoming too slow at millions of vectors. Approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search returns almost-the-best results in sublinear time by not examining every vector. Choosing exact vs ANN is a recall-versus-latency trade-off that defines how your store scales.
subtopics.example:
import numpy as np

def brute_force(query, vectors, k):
    # exact: score against EVERY vector -> O(n) per query
    sims = [float(query @ v / (np.linalg.norm(query) * np.linalg.norm(v)))
            for v in vectors]
    order = np.argsort(sims)[::-1][:k]
    return [(int(i), round(sims[i], 3)) for i in order]

# fine for thousands; too slow for tens of millions per query

subtopics.title: HNSW and IVF intuition
subtopics.explanation: HNSW builds a layered graph where each vector links to nearby vectors, so a query greedily hops toward its neighborhood, skipping most of the dataset. IVF first clusters vectors into cells and, at query time, searches only the few cells nearest the query. Both prune the search space so you compare against a small candidate set instead of everything — that pruning is the core trick behind fast vector search.
subtopics.example:
# HNSW: navigable graph, follow edges toward the query
#   start high in the graph, descend, hop to nearer neighbors
#   tune: M (edges/node), ef_search (candidates explored)
#
# IVF: partition into `nlist` cells (centroids), probe `nprobe` of them
#   more nprobe -> higher recall, slower query
index_params = {"type": "hnsw", "M": 16, "ef_search": 64}
ivf_params   = {"type": "ivf", "nlist": 1024, "nprobe": 8}

subtopics.title: Top-k retrieval
subtopics.explanation: A query returns the k most similar records, ranked by similarity score, where k is how many passages you'll feed the generator. Small k keeps the prompt focused and cheap but risks missing the answer; large k improves recall but adds noise and tokens. Tuning k is how you balance retrieval recall against prompt size in the generate step.
subtopics.example:
hits = store.query(embed("refund window"), k=3)
for h in hits:
    print(round(h["score"], 3), h["id"], "->", h["text"])
# 0.91 doc.md::c0 -> refunds take 14 days
# 0.42 doc.md::c1 -> store opens at 9am
# feed the top-k texts into the generator's prompt as context

subtopics.title: Metadata filtering
subtopics.explanation: Beyond similarity, you constrain results by metadata — only this tenant's docs, only the current product version, only published pages — either before or during the search. Filtering enforces access control and relevance that pure vector similarity can't express. Combining a filter with top-k is what makes retrieval both correct and safe in multi-tenant systems.
subtopics.example:
hits = store.query(
    embed("refund window"),
    k=3,
    where={"product": "pro", "published": True},  # metadata filter
)
# only vectors whose metadata matches are eligible;
# prevents leaking another tenant's or an unpublished chunk

foundations.overview: After chunking and embedding, retrieval needs a place to store vectors and a way to search them quickly. A vector store keeps each embedding together with its source text, metadata, and a stable id, exposing two operations: upsert (add or update records) and query (return the top-k most similar to an embedded query). The simplest search is brute force — score the query against every vector by cosine and sort — which is exact but scales linearly and becomes too slow at millions of vectors. Production stores instead build approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes: HNSW constructs a navigable small-world graph so a query greedily hops toward its neighborhood, while IVF clusters vectors into cells and probes only the few nearest cells. Both prune the candidate set to gain sublinear speed at the cost of occasionally missing a true neighbor, a recall-versus-latency knob you tune (ef_search, nprobe). Queries return the top-k results ranked by score, where k balances recall against prompt size, and metadata filtering scopes results by tenant, version, or permission for correctness and access control. This store is the retrieval engine every RAG system queries on each request.
foundations.formalDefinition: A vector store is a database that indexes fixed-dimensional embedding vectors (with associated text and metadata) to support approximate or exact k-nearest-neighbor queries under a similarity metric such as cosine. An ANN index (e.g. HNSW graph or IVF clustering) is a data structure that answers top-k similarity queries in sublinear time by restricting comparisons to a pruned candidate set, trading recall for speed.
foundations.whyItMatters: Retrieval runs on every RAG request, so its speed and recall directly set the system's latency, cost, and answer quality. The vector store and its index are what make semantic search over millions of chunks fast enough for interactive use while still returning the right passages.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the store as a library and ANN as a smart floor plan. Brute force is reading every book's spine to find the closest match; HNSW is following signposts from section to nearer section until you're in the right aisle; IVF is going straight to the two or three shelves whose labels match your topic and only scanning those. Metadata filtering is a librarian who first restricts you to the wing you're allowed into.
foundations.performanceImpact: Brute force is O(n) per query and fine up to tens of thousands of vectors; ANN indexes give roughly logarithmic query cost at the price of index build time, extra memory, and a tunable recall gap. Raising ef_search/nprobe or k improves recall but increases latency and, for k, prompt token cost downstream.
commonUseCases: Top-k semantic retrieval on every RAG query
Scaling search to millions of chunks with HNSW/IVF

commonMisconceptions.myth: ANN returns the exact nearest neighbors.
commonMisconceptions.reality: ANN returns approximate neighbors — it may occasionally miss a true top-k result. You trade a small recall gap (tunable via ef_search/nprobe) for large speed gains.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A bigger k always gives better answers.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Large k adds low-relevance chunks and tokens that can distract the generator and raise cost. There's a sweet spot; more context is not automatically better.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Metadata filtering is just a nice-to-have.
commonMisconceptions.reality: In multi-tenant or permissioned systems it's a correctness and security requirement — without it a query can surface another tenant's or an unpublished chunk.

codeLab.title: Build a filterable top-k vector store
codeLab.instructions: Implement a MiniStore class with two methods. upsert(records) adds records where each record is a dict with keys id, vector (list of floats), text, and metadata (dict); re-upserting the same id must UPDATE in place, not duplicate. query(vector, k, where=None) returns the top-k records by cosine similarity, considering only records whose metadata matches every key/value in `where` (None means no filter). Each returned item must be a dict with id, text, and score. Ties may be in any order. Complete the class so the harness passes.
codeLab.testHarness:
s = MiniStore()
s.upsert([
    {"id": "c0", "vector": [1, 0, 0], "text": "refund", "metadata": {"t": "a"}},
    {"id": "c1", "vector": [0, 1, 0], "text": "hours",  "metadata": {"t": "a"}},
    {"id": "c2", "vector": [1, 0, 0], "text": "refund2", "metadata": {"t": "b"}},
])
# top-1 for a refund-like query is a refund chunk
top = s.query([1, 0, 0], k=1)
assert top[0]["text"] in ("refund", "refund2"), top
# metadata filter restricts eligible records
fa = s.query([1, 0, 0], k=5, where={"t": "a"})
assert {h["id"] for h in fa} == {"c0", "c1"}, fa
assert fa[0]["id"] == "c0", fa   # refund outranks hours for this query
# re-upsert updates in place, no duplicate id
s.upsert([{"id": "c0", "vector": [0, 0, 1], "text": "changed", "metadata": {"t": "a"}}])
all_ids = [h["id"] for h in s.query([0, 0, 1], k=10)]
assert all_ids.count("c0") == 1, all_ids
assert s.query([0, 0, 1], k=1)[0]["text"] == "changed"
print("all tests passed")
hints: Store records in a dict keyed by id so re-upserting the same id overwrites instead of appending.
Cosine = (a dot b) / (||a|| * ||b||); guard against a zero-norm vector to avoid dividing by zero.
Apply the `where` filter (all key/values must match the record's metadata) before scoring, then sort by score descending and slice the first k.

debuggingLab.title: The filter ran after top-k, leaking wrong-tenant chunks
debuggingLab.scenario: A multi-tenant support bot occasionally shows one customer text from another customer's docs. The retrieval code takes the global top-k by similarity first and only then drops results whose tenant doesn't match. When a query's true nearest neighbors all belong to other tenants, the post-filter removes them and returns fewer (or zero) of the requesting tenant's chunks — and in an earlier version it forgot to filter one branch entirely, leaking cross-tenant text.
debuggingLab.diagnosis: Filtering after top-k is both a recall bug and a security bug. Recall: the ANN search spends its k budget on globally-nearest vectors that may all belong to other tenants, so after removing them you're left with too few of the right tenant's chunks. Security: the filter lives in application code separate from the query, so any forgotten branch leaks another tenant's text. The tenant constraint must be part of the search itself, not a fragile afterthought.

fix.code:
def retrieve(store, q, k, tenant):
    # push the tenant constraint INTO the query so only eligible
    # vectors compete for the k slots -- correct recall AND isolation
    return store.query(q, k=k, where={"tenant": tenant})

# the store scores only this tenant's vectors, so:
#  - k slots are filled from eligible chunks (recall restored)
#  - other tenants' chunks can never appear (isolation enforced)

debuggingLab.lesson: Never filter after ranking when the filter is a correctness or security boundary. Push metadata constraints into the query so only eligible vectors compete for the top-k slots: this both preserves recall (the k budget isn't wasted on ineligible results) and guarantees isolation (ineligible chunks can never surface). Treat tenant/permission filters as part of the index query contract, not application-layer cleanup.
debuggingLab.expectedOutput: only the requesting tenant's chunks, up to k

productionDeepDive.architecture: Sit the vector store behind a retrieval service that owns embedding the query, applying mandatory metadata filters (tenant/permission), running the ANN query, and returning typed hits with text and citation metadata. Keep the embedding model, index type, and its parameters versioned with the index so a re-embed or index rebuild is a controlled migration. Separate the write path (chunk -> embed -> upsert) from the read path so ingestion spikes don't degrade query latency.
productionDeepDive.performance: Choose the index for scale: brute force or a flat index up to tens of thousands of vectors, HNSW for low-latency high-recall at moderate scale, IVF (or IVF+PQ) for very large corpora where memory matters. Tune ef_search/nprobe to hit a target recall, cap k to what the generator actually needs, and warm/keep the index in memory to avoid cold-start latency.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Make upserts idempotent via stable ids so re-ingestion updates rather than duplicates, and rebuild or compact the index on a schedule since heavy deletes/updates degrade ANN structures over time. Handle the empty-result case explicitly (no eligible chunks after filtering) rather than passing an empty context to the generator, and validate query vector dimensionality matches the index.
productionDeepDive.observability: Track query latency percentiles, recall against a periodic exact-search sample, top-k score distributions, and the rate of empty or low-score results. A drift in score distribution or a rising empty-result rate signals index degradation, an embedder change, or a filter that's too strict — all before users report bad answers.
productionDeepDive.security: Metadata filtering is an access-control boundary: enforce tenant/permission filters inside the query, never as post-ranking application code that can be bypassed or forgotten. Validate and constrain filter inputs so a caller can't broaden their own scope, and consider per-tenant namespaces/collections for hard isolation rather than relying solely on a metadata field.
productionDeepDive.cost: Index memory and query volume dominate cost. Compress vectors (product quantization) and pick IVF for huge corpora to cut RAM, cache embeddings and frequent query results, and keep k small since every retrieved chunk adds generator tokens. Right-sizing ef_search/nprobe avoids paying for recall beyond what improves answers.

caseStudies.company: A B2B SaaS platform with per-customer knowledge bases
caseStudies.problem: Their RAG search grew slow past a few hundred thousand chunks using brute-force cosine, and a post-ranking tenant filter both returned too few results and, in one code path, leaked another customer's text.
caseStudies.solution: They moved to an HNSW index with tuned ef_search for sub-100ms queries, pushed the tenant filter into the query so only a customer's own vectors were eligible, added per-tenant namespaces for hard isolation, and instrumented recall against periodic exact-search samples.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: HNSW added index build time and memory and introduced a small, tunable recall gap versus exact search; in exchange query latency dropped sharply at scale and cross-tenant leakage became structurally impossible.
caseStudies.lessons: Pick the index for your scale and always enforce permission filters inside the query — post-ranking filtering silently hurts recall and can leak data, while in-query filtering fixes both.

checkpoints.prompt: What does an approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) index trade for its speed?
options: A small, tunable chance of missing a true top-k neighbor, in exchange for sublinear query time
checkpoints.explanation: ANN prunes the candidate set (via a graph or clustering) so it doesn't examine every vector, gaining sublinear speed at the cost of an occasional missed neighbor — a recall gap you tune with ef_search/nprobe.

checkpoints.prompt: In a multi-tenant system, where should a tenant filter be applied?
options: After taking the global top-k, in application code
Inside the query, so only the tenant's vectors compete for the top-k slots
It doesn't matter as long as it's applied somewhere
checkpoints.explanation: Filtering after ranking wastes the k budget on ineligible results (hurting recall) and can leak data if a code path forgets it. Pushing the filter into the query preserves recall and structurally enforces isolation.

checkpoints.prompt: Given identical vectors but different metadata, what does this print?
checkpoints.code:
recs = [
  {"id": "a", "vector": [1, 0], "metadata": {"t": "x"}},
  {"id": "b", "vector": [1, 0], "metadata": {"t": "y"}},
]
eligible = [r["id"] for r in recs if r["metadata"]["t"] == "x"]
print(eligible)
checkpoints.explanation: Similarity alone can't separate identical vectors; only the metadata filter for t == 'x' does, leaving just record 'a'. This is why metadata filtering, not similarity, enforces isolation.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the cosine so a zero-norm vector doesn't crash the query with a divide-by-zero.
checkpoints.codeBefore:
def cosine(a, b):
    import numpy as np
    a, b = np.array(a), np.array(b)
    denom = np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b)
    return float(a @ b / denom) if
checkpoints.explanation: If either vector has zero norm, `denom` is 0 and dividing would raise/produce nan. Guarding `if denom` returns 0.0 similarity for a degenerate vector instead of crashing the query.

theory.question: What is a vector store and how do HNSW and IVF make it fast at scale?
theory.directAnswer: A vector store indexes embeddings with their text and metadata and answers top-k similarity queries. Brute force scores every vector (O(n)), too slow at scale, so ANN indexes prune the search: HNSW builds a navigable graph so a query hops toward its neighborhood, and IVF clusters vectors into cells and probes only the few nearest cells. Both compare against a small candidate set for sublinear speed, trading a tunable recall gap.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A specialized database for embeddings supporting upsert and k-nearest-neighbor query under a similarity metric like cosine.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Exact search is linear in corpus size and can't meet interactive latency at millions of vectors; ANN indexes make semantic search fast enough for production.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: HNSW: a layered proximity graph greedily traversed from coarse to fine, tuned by M and ef_search. IVF: k-means cells (nlist) with nprobe cells searched per query. More ef_search/nprobe raises recall and latency.

theory.whyImportant: Retrieval runs on every request, so the index choice sets latency, cost, and recall — the levers that most shape a RAG system's feel and quality.
theory.realWorldExample: A corpus that was fine with brute force at 50k chunks slowed badly at millions; switching to HNSW with tuned ef_search restored sub-100ms queries at high recall.

followUps.question: When is brute force actually fine?
followUps.answer: Up to roughly tens of thousands of vectors, where exact O(n) search is still fast and you avoid ANN's build cost, memory, and recall gap.

followUps.question: How do you choose between HNSW and IVF?
followUps.answer: HNSW for low-latency high-recall at moderate scale; IVF (often with product quantization) when the corpus is huge and memory is the binding constraint.

theory.question: How do you choose k for top-k retrieval, and what are the trade-offs?
theory.directAnswer: k is how many passages you feed the generator. Too small risks missing the chunk that contains the answer (low recall); too large adds low-relevance chunks that distract the model and inflate token cost. You pick the smallest k that reliably includes the answer on an eval set, often with reranking to keep quality while shrinking k.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A retrieval parameter controlling how many nearest neighbors are returned and passed as context.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: There's tension between recall (need enough chunks to include the answer) and precision/cost (too many chunks add noise and tokens).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Measure answer accuracy and retrieval-hit rate across k values on a held-out QA set; increase k until hit-rate plateaus, then optionally rerank the retrieved set and truncate to the top few for the prompt.

theory.whyImportant: k directly trades answer recall against prompt cost and distraction, making it a core tuning knob for both quality and spend.
theory.realWorldExample: Raising k from 3 to 8 lifted hit-rate, but answers got noisier and costlier; adding a reranker let them retrieve 20 and prompt with the best 4, getting recall and precision.

followUps.question: How does reranking relate to k?
followUps.answer: Retrieve a larger candidate set for recall, then rerank and keep only the top few for the prompt, decoupling recall (retrieval k) from context size.

followUps.question: Does bigger k always cost more?
followUps.answer: Yes downstream — each extra chunk adds generator input tokens and can dilute the answer, so more context is not automatically better.

scenario.question: Your vector search is fast but recall dropped after you scaled from 100k to 5M chunks and switched to an ANN index. How do you diagnose and restore recall?
scenario.directAnswer: Measure ANN recall against a periodic exact (brute-force) sample to quantify the gap, then raise the recall knobs (ef_search for HNSW, nprobe for IVF) to your target, rebuild/compact the index if deletes degraded it, and verify query latency stays within budget. If memory-bound, choose IVF with quantization and re-tune.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An ANN recall-versus-latency tuning problem exposed by scaling the corpus.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: ANN indexes approximate; default parameters that gave good recall at 100k may probe too small a candidate set at 5M, and churn from updates degrades graph/cluster quality.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Sample queries, compute exact top-k, compare to ANN results to get recall, increase ef_search/nprobe until recall meets target, watch the latency cost, and rebuild if the index has drifted from heavy writes.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows treating recall as a measurable, tunable quantity rather than assuming ANN 'just works', which is essential when scaling RAG.
scenario.realWorldExample: Recall had quietly fallen to ~85% after scaling; raising ef_search restored it to ~98% with only a modest latency increase, and scheduling index compaction stopped further drift.

followUps.question: How do you measure ANN recall in production?
followUps.answer: Periodically run a sample of queries through exact brute-force search and compare the top-k overlap with the ANN results.

followUps.question: Why can recall degrade over time even with fixed params?
followUps.answer: Heavy deletes and updates fragment the graph or clusters; scheduled rebuilds/compaction restore the index structure and recall.

coding.question: Implement top-k cosine retrieval over an in-memory list of records with an optional metadata filter applied inside the search.
coding.thoughtProcess: I compute cosine per candidate but only for records that pass the metadata filter, so the filter is part of the search rather than post-ranking (correct recall and isolation). I guard a zero norm to avoid divide-by-zero, sort descending by score, and slice the first k. Returning id/text/score keeps results citable.

solution.code:
import numpy as np

def retrieve(records, query, k, where=None):
    where = where or {}
    q = np.array(query, dtype=float)
    qn = np.linalg.norm(q)
    hits = []
    for r in records:
        meta = r.get("metadata", {})
        if not all(meta.get(key) == val for key, val in where.items()):
            continue                         # filter inside the search
        v = np.array(r["vector"], dtype=float)
        denom = qn * np.linalg.norm(v)
        score = float(q @ v / denom) if denom else 0.0
        hits.append({"id": r["id"], "text": r["text"], "score": score})
    hits.sort(key=lambda h: h["score"], reverse=True)
    return hits[:k]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    recs = [
        {"id": "c0", "vector": [1, 0], "text": "refund", "metadata": {"t": "a"}},
        {"id": "c1", "vector": [1, 0], "text": "other",  "metadata": {"t": "b"}},
    ]
    print([h["id"] for h in retrieve(recs, [1, 0], k=5, where={"t": "a"})])

lineByLine: Normalize the query once (qn) so it isn't recomputed per record.
For each record, the metadata filter is checked first; non-matching records are skipped before scoring, keeping the filter inside the search.
Cosine = q·v / (||q|| ||v||), with a guard returning 0.0 when either norm is zero to avoid divide-by-zero.
Matching records are collected as citable hits with id, text, and score.
Sorting descending by score and slicing [:k] yields the top-k.
The __main__ block shows identical vectors separated only by the metadata filter, returning just tenant 'a'.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n * d) — one dot product of dimension d over n candidate records, plus O(n log n) for the sort.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the hits list (or O(k) if you use a heap of size k instead of sorting).

followUps.question: How would you avoid sorting all n hits?
followUps.answer: Maintain a size-k min-heap of the best scores so far, giving O(n log k) instead of O(n log n) — meaningful when n is large and k is small.

followUps.question: Why filter inside the search rather than after?
followUps.answer: Post-ranking filtering wastes the k budget on ineligible results (hurting recall) and can leak data if a path forgets it; in-search filtering fixes both.

keyTakeaways: A vector store keeps each embedding with its text, metadata, and a stable id, and answers top-k similarity queries via upsert/query.
Brute force is exact but O(n); ANN indexes (HNSW graph, IVF clustering) prune the candidate set for sublinear speed at a tunable recall cost.
Tune recall knobs (ef_search, nprobe) and k against an eval set: bigger raises recall but adds latency, and larger k adds prompt tokens and noise.
Push metadata filters into the query so only eligible vectors compete for the top-k — this preserves recall and enforces multi-tenant isolation.
Retrieval runs on every RAG request, so index choice and parameters set the system's latency, cost, and answer quality.
